nameStory: This bright cup fungus earned its "orange peel" nickname from its vivid orange interior that looks remarkably like a discarded citrus rind scattered on the forest floor. The "spring" part of its name reflects its unique timing - it's one of the first colorful fungi to appear after snowmelt, bringing a splash of warmth to the still-brown landscape.
description: The Spring Orange Peel Fungus is a cup-shaped fungus that looks like someone scattered bright orange citrus peels across the forest floor. These shallow, bowl-like cups typically grow up to about 1.5 inches across, with brilliant orange interiors that fade to paler orange on the outside. As they age or get damaged, you'll often notice olive-green staining around the edges, giving them a bruised appearance.

idTips.label: Cup Shape
idTips.description: Shallow, bowl-like cups that feel somewhat firm and rubbery to the touch, not fragile like many other cup fungi

idTips.label: Bright Orange Interior
idTips.description: Vivid orange inner surface that catches your eye from a distance, looking remarkably like fresh orange peel

idTips.label: Olive-Green Staining
idTips.description: Older specimens develop distinctive olive or greenish discoloration, especially around the rim where they've been damaged

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 1-2 inches across, small enough to fit comfortably in your palm

idTips.label: Ground Habitat
idTips.description: Always found directly on the ground among leaf litter and debris, never growing on wood

habitat: Look for these colorful cups on the ground in coniferous forests, particularly near spruce, fir, and pine trees. They grow directly in the forest litter and organic debris, often partially hidden among fallen needles and decaying leaves. In New England, they're most common in the cooler, moister coniferous forests of northern Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine.

seasonality.spring: This is when you'll find them! They appear in early spring right after snowmelt, usually March through May, making them one of the earliest colorful fungi of the year.
seasonality.summer: Completely absent - they've finished their brief fruiting season and won't return until next spring.
seasonality.fall: Not found during autumn, despite this being peak mushroom season for most other fungi.
seasonality.winter: Hidden underground, waiting for the snow to melt before emerging again next spring.

funFact: This cheerful spring fungus has a secret dark side - its invisible spore stage actually attacks and kills dormant Sitka spruce seeds, acting as a stealth plant pathogen while masquerading as a harmless forest decorator!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other orange cup fungi, but the spring timing is a dead giveaway - if you find bright orange cups right after snowmelt, it's almost certainly this species. Other orange cups typically fruit in summer or fall, not spring.
contextualKnowledge: Don't be fooled by the common name into thinking this has anything to do with citrus fruits - the "orange peel" refers purely to the color and appearance, not any botanical relationship to orange trees.
compareHints: This is the only species in its genus Caloscypha, making it unique among New England fungi. Compared to other orange cup fungi in the region, it stands out for its early spring emergence right after snowmelt, while most similar-looking species fruit much later in the year. The characteristic olive-green bruising on older specimens is also distinctive among orange cup fungi.
